posts.quote: THE HYMN BOARD HAD THE SAME FOUR NUMBERS ON IT EVERY SUNDAY, AND THE WHOLE CONGREGATION STILL LOOKED UP TO CHECK.
posts.caption: The hymn board hung on the wall at the front of the church, a little walnut frame with a row of white numbers slid into slots. Every Sunday the usher changed them just before the service, and every Sunday it came out the same four numbers, or close enough. The hymnals were in the racks anyway, with the pages worn soft at all the usual spots. Still, when the organ finished its opening notes, the whole congregation tipped their heads back to check the board. Somebody's grandmother would nod once, as if to confirm the church was running on schedule. Then we all stood up and sang the hymn we could have sung blindfolded.
posts.first: My father sat on the aisle and never once looked at the board. He found the page by feel, and he was always a half-beat ahead of everyone else on the first line. I think he just liked knowing where he was in the world.

posts.quote: THE WASHBOARD STAYED ON THE BACK PORCH LONG AFTER THE WASHER ARRIVED, BECAUSE GRANDMA DIDN'T TRUST THE NEW MACHINE.
posts.caption: The washing machine came to our house the year I turned seven, a big white thing that hummed in the corner of the back porch. Grandma admired it, ran her hand over the top, and said it was a fine piece of work. Then she hung her washboard back on its nail on the wall beside it, right where it had always been. Anything delicate, anything stained, and anything belonging to my grandfather got scrubbed on the board with a bar of yellow soap. The machine got the sheets and the towels, and the board got the things she cared about. It hung there for the rest of her life, the zinc ridges worn smooth in the middle where her knuckles had been.
posts.first: I have that washboard in my laundry room now, hanging on a nail. I've never once used it, but I can't make myself take it down. It still smells faintly of yellow soap if you put your nose close to the frame.

posts.quote: THE BACK OF THE COMIC BOOK / A TINY SUBMARINE, A PAIR OF TRICK GLASSES, AND SIX WEEKS OF WAITING BY THE MAILBOX
posts.caption: The ads on the back of the comic book were the real reading. You could get a tiny submarine, a pair of glasses that supposedly let you see through things, or a whole army of plastic soldiers, all for a dollar and a stamp. You filled out the coupon in pencil, pressed a dollar bill flat in the envelope, and walked it to the mailbox like it was a state secret. Then came the waiting, which was six to eight weeks and felt like a school year. Every afternoon you checked the mailbox the minute you got home. What finally showed up was always smaller than the picture, and you loved it anyway.
posts.first: I sent away for a submarine once and checked that mailbox every day for nearly two months. When it came, it was about the size of a bar of soap, and it did not dive. I played with it in the bathtub anyway until the summer was over.

posts.quote: The front hall closet smelled like wet wool, rubber boots, and a little bit like every winter you ever had.
posts.first: Ours was behind the front door, and it held six pairs of boots, one umbrella nobody claimed, and my father's hunting cap. The smell came out every time somebody opened it. I'd know it anywhere.

posts.quote: WE DRESSED THE SCARECROW IN DAD'S OLD OVERALLS, AND THE CROWS TREATED HIM LIKE A FRIEND.
posts.caption: Dad took the scarecrow job seriously every fall. He handed over his oldest pair of overalls, the ones with the patched knees, and told us to stuff them with straw from the barn. We tied the sleeves shut with baling twine, gave him a burlap sack for a head, and set a straw hat on top with a hole in the brim. We stood him up at the corner of the garden and felt like we'd built a guard dog. By noon there were three crows sitting on his shoulders. They stayed there all season, as comfortable as if he'd hired them.
posts.first: Dad stood out in the garden that evening with his hands on his hips, looking at those crows. He said, "Well, he's got a crew now," and went in to wash up. We lost most of that first row of corn.

posts.quote: THE CIDER STAND RAN ON A COFFEE CAN AND TRUST, AND THE CAN WAS ALWAYS FULL AT THE END OF THE DAY.
posts.caption: Out on the county road past the orchard, a plank table sat under a maple every fall, stacked with gallon jugs of cider and a bushel of apples on each end. Nobody ever worked it. A coffee can with a slit cut in the plastic lid sat in the middle, and the price was lettered on a piece of cardboard in house paint. You took a jug, slid your money through the slot, and drove off with the whole back seat smelling like October. The farmer came by after supper to empty the can and restock the table. In all those years I never heard of a single dollar going missing.
posts.first: My mother always made us roll the windows down on the drive home, even when it was cold. She said you had to let the cider smell go all the way through the car. I can still hear that jug sloshing on the back floor every time we hit the gravel.

posts.quote: THE TURKEY WENT IN BEFORE SUNRISE, AND DAD GUARDED THE OVEN LIKE IT OWED HIM MONEY.
posts.caption: The turkey went into the oven before sunrise, and by six the whole house was awake because of it. Dad took up his post in the kitchen doorway in his undershirt and slippers, a dish towel over one shoulder, like a man guarding a bank. Every twenty minutes he opened the oven door and basted the bird with a spoon, and every twenty minutes my mother told him to stop opening the oven door. Neither one of them gave an inch. When we sat down at two o'clock it was the best turkey of the decade, and my father took full credit for it in front of everybody. Mom just passed the gravy and let him have it.
posts.first: Mom kept that same roasting pan for forty years, a speckled blue one with a dent in the lid. Dad always said the dent was where the turkey fought back. I've got the pan now, and the dent is still there.

posts.quote: THE LOCKER / A COMBINATION YOU MEMORIZED, A DENTED DOOR, AND A MIRROR THE SIZE OF A POSTCARD
posts.caption: Your locker was the first place in the world that was only yours, at least as far as the school was concerned. It came with a three-number combination you practiced on the bus until your fingers knew it without thinking. The door had a dent from somebody's shoulder, and the inside smelled like gym socks and an orange from October. A mirror the size of a postcard hung on the inside, held up by a magnet, and that mirror got more of your attention than any textbook. You stacked your books by size and slammed the door with your hip. That slam was the sound of the whole hallway between classes.
posts.first: I forgot my combination on the first day of ninth grade and stood there turning the dial for ten minutes. A senior walked by, reached over, and opened it with one knock in the right spot. He never said a word, and I've been grateful ever since.

posts.quote: Every old kitchen had one wobbly chair, and the family had a quiet agreement about who sat in it.
posts.first: At our house it was the one by the stove, and it was my brother's. He knew exactly how far to lean to keep it from rocking. When he left for the service, nobody else sat in it for a month.

posts.quote: THE ALUMINUM LAWN CHAIR LEFT A WOVEN PATTERN ON THE BACKS OF YOUR LEGS, AND YOU WORE IT LIKE A SUMMER TATTOO.
posts.caption: The folding aluminum lawn chair came out of the garage the first warm Saturday of the year, and the whole neighborhood was sitting in them by supper. They were woven with green and white plastic webbing that squeaked when you sat down and pinched the back of your legs when you stood up. After one afternoon in a pair of shorts you had a perfect waffle pattern printed across your thighs. Nobody minded. You compared it with the neighbor kid's like a medal, and by Monday it had faded. Then the next warm weekend came and you earned a fresh set.
posts.first: Ours had a broken strap on one arm that my father fixed every spring with a piece of green garden twine. It held for twenty summers. I'd still know that squeak anywhere.
